newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Diplomats see no end to "EU company statute" row.
newsitem.headline: Diplomats see no end to "EU company statute" row.

text.p: European Union social affairs ministers will try to break a long-standing deadlock this weekend over plans to allow firms to set up as European companies, but diplomats say chances of progress are slim.

"I'm not sure I see a breakthrough," one British diplomat told Reuters, predicting that the informal ministerial meeting in Echternach, Luxembourg, on Friday and Saturday would simply reaffirm the conflict between British and German views.
The European Commission's proposal for a European company statute, designed to make life easier for industry and save costs, has been deadlocked for more than 20 years.
The statute would allow a firm to set up as a "European company" operating on a Europe-wide basis, eliminating the need to set up a network of costly subsidiaries.

The main stumbling block has been the provisions on worker participation in company decisions, with Bonn promoting its own system of 50-50 "co-determination" between employees and managers and London arguing there should be no mandatory rules.

The Commission said in May it saw chances of ending the row in the form of proposals from a high-level expert group headed by Etienne Davignon, the chairman of Belgian holding company Societe Generale and a former European commissioner.
The Davignon group suggested unions and employers should first try to agree on the worker involvement on the board of each individual European companies.
Only in the absence of agreement would a set of reference rules apply, obliging companies to give employees' representatives a fifth of the seats on their board.

The proposal, which one British diplomat said was designed largely to address Bonn's fear "that firms would be able to wriggle out of their co-determination (obligations) by setting up as a European company", has not fully satisfied either side.
"We think its absolutely necessary to have co-determination in the European company system," a German diplomat told Reuters.

"The (Davignon) proposal to do it in a negotiated way is a good idea but the rule that one fifth of (board members) should be employees' representatives... is not satisfactory because it doesn't go as far as our own system," he explained.

British diplomats, for their part, argue that the Davignon proposals go too far, forcing the hand of firms operating in countries that do not have a tradition of worker participation, such as Britain and Ireland.
Britain is still promoting a "better buy" system, even though this has been rejected by the Davignon group.
Such a system would oblige European companies to adopt the most extensive worker participation rules applying in the EU member states in which they operate.
This would force an Anglo-German firm to accept co- determination but would allow an Anglo-Irish company to retain its current model.
Davignon's idea of imposing mandatory minimum rules would simply undermine the -- very useful -- idea of a European company statute, one British diplomat said.
"As long as the statute remains optional, building in provisions that would make it unattractive in one member state or other would undermine the idea," he said.
He predicted Davignon's proposals would not get enough support from EU governments to become law and suggested other options should be explored.
